questions.stem:
The bar below is divided into 8 equal parts.

![Bar of 8 equal parts, 5 shaded](asset:q1-fig)

(a) What fraction of the bar is shaded? (b) What fraction is unshaded? (c) If the whole bar stands for 40 marbles, how many marbles does the shaded part represent?
questions.solution: The bar has 8 equal parts with 5 shaded. (a) Shaded = $\frac{5}{8}$. (b) Unshaded = $\frac{3}{8}$. (c) 40 × $\frac{5}{8}$ = **25 marbles**.

fields.Skill focus: Reading a fraction as part of a whole; finding a part from the whole, and recovering the whole from a part.

questions.stem: In a class, $\frac{3}{7}$ of the students are boys. There are exactly 12 boys. How many students are in the class, and how many are girls?
questions.solution: $\frac{3}{7}$ of the class = 12, so the whole = 12 × $\frac{7}{3}$ = **28 students**; girls = 28 − 12 = **16**.

questions.stem: A ribbon is cut into equal pieces. Four of those pieces together make up $\frac{4}{9}$ of the whole ribbon. Into how many equal pieces is the ribbon cut, and what fraction of the ribbon is one piece?
questions.solution: 4 pieces make $\frac{4}{9}$, so 1 piece = $\frac{1}{9}$ and the ribbon is cut into **9 equal pieces**.

questions.stem: Priya reads $\frac{1}{4}$ of a book on Monday and 40 more pages on Tuesday. She has now read exactly half the book. How many pages does the book have?
questions.solution: Monday $\frac{1}{4}$ plus 40 pages equals half, so 40 pages = $\frac{1}{2}$ − $\frac{1}{4}$ = $\frac{1}{4}$ of the book ⇒ book = **160 pages**.

questions.stem: On a farm, $\frac{5}{9}$ of the animals are chickens and the rest are goats. There are 24 more chickens than goats. How many animals are on the farm?
questions.solution: Chickens $\frac{5}{9}$, goats $\frac{4}{9}$; the difference $\frac{1}{9}$ = 24, so total = **216 animals** (120 chickens, 96 goats).

questions.stem: At a school, $\frac{4}{7}$ of the pupils walk to school and the rest come by bus. Next term, 30 pupils who used to take the bus start walking instead, and now $\frac{5}{7}$ of the pupils walk. The total number of pupils is unchanged. How many pupils attend the school?
questions.solution: Walkers rise from $\frac{4}{7}$ to $\frac{5}{7}$, an increase of $\frac{1}{7}$ = 30 pupils ⇒ total = **210 pupils**. (Check: 120→150 walk, 90→60 bus.)

questions.stem: A collection of coins is made of gold, silver and bronze. Exactly $\frac{1}{2}$ of the coins are bronze. Of the coins that are *not* bronze, $\frac{2}{3}$ are silver. There are 8 gold coins. How many coins are there altogether, and how many are silver?
questions.solution: Bronze = $\frac{1}{2}$. Of the other $\frac{1}{2}$, silver is $\frac{2}{3}$ (= $\frac{1}{3}$ of all) and gold is $\frac{1}{3}$ of that half (= $\frac{1}{6}$ of all). So $\frac{1}{6}$ = 8 ⇒ total = **48 coins**; silver = $\frac{1}{3}$ × 48 = **16**.

questions.stem:
Find $\frac{2}{3}$ of $\frac{3}{4}$. Use the area model below to explain your answer.

![Area model: unit square in a 4 by 3 grid, three columns lightly shaded, two rows of those columns darkly shaded](asset:q10-fig)

*Light shading covers $\frac{3}{4}$ (3 of 4 columns). The dark overlay covers $\frac{2}{3}$ of that region — the 6 double-shaded cells out of 12.*
questions.solution: $\frac{2}{3}$ × $\frac{3}{4}$ = $\frac{6}{12}$ = **$\frac{1}{2}$**. In the model, the double-shaded region is 6 of the 12 cells.

questions.stem: A pizza has $\frac{3}{4}$ of it left. Sam eats $\frac{1}{3}$ of what is left. What fraction of the whole pizza did Sam eat, and what fraction of the whole pizza now remains?
questions.solution: Sam eats $\frac{1}{3}$ × $\frac{3}{4}$ = **$\frac{1}{4}$** of the whole; remaining = $\frac{3}{4}$ − $\frac{1}{4}$ = **$\frac{1}{2}$**.

questions.stem: A field is $\frac{5}{6}$ planted. Of the planted part, $\frac{3}{10}$ is wheat. The wheat covers 25 m². What is the area of the whole field?
questions.solution: Wheat fraction of the field = $\frac{3}{10}$ × $\frac{5}{6}$ = $\frac{1}{4}$. So $\frac{1}{4}$ = 25 m² ⇒ field = **100 m²**.

questions.stem: Some sweets are shared out. First $\frac{1}{3}$ of them are given to Ann. Of the remainder, $\frac{1}{4}$ are given to Ben. Of what is then left, $\frac{2}{5}$ are given to Cara. After this, 27 sweets remain. How many sweets were there at the start, and how many did Ben receive?

questions.stem:
A frog starts at 0. Each jump takes it exactly $\frac{1}{2}$ of the remaining distance to the point 1. So after jump 1 it is at $\frac{1}{2}$, after jump 2 at $\frac{3}{4}$, and so on.

![Number line showing frog jumps landing at one half, three quarters, seven eighths, fifteen sixteenths](asset:q45-fig)

(a) Where is the frog after the 4th jump? (b) What fraction of the way to 1 is still left after the 4th jump? (c) Will the frog ever land exactly on 1? Explain.
questions.solution: After n jumps the frog is at 1 − ($\frac{1}{2}$)<sup>n</sup>. (a) 1 − $\frac{1}{16}$ = **$\frac{15}{16}$**. (b) Left = **$\frac{1}{16}$**. (c) **No** — ($\frac{1}{2}$)<sup>n</sup> is always greater than 0, so the position is always less than 1.

questions.solution: Rates: A = $\frac{1}{4}$/h, B = $\frac{1}{6}$/h; net = $\frac{1}{4}$ − $\frac{1}{6}$ = $\frac{1}{12}$/h \> 0, so it **fills**. From $\frac{1}{2}$ to $\frac{5}{6}$ needs $\frac{1}{3}$; time = $\frac{1}{3}$ ÷ $\frac{1}{12}$ = **4 hours**.

(c) After how many total hours does the tank first return to empty (reach 0)?
questions.solution: (a) After hour 1: $\frac{5}{12}$ + $\frac{1}{4}$ = **$\frac{2}{3}$**. (b) With Z open: $\frac{5}{12}$ + $\frac{3}{12}$ − $\frac{10}{12}$ = **−$\frac{1}{6}$ per hour**. questions.stem: Three coin types: gold, silver, bronze. One gold balances two silver; one silver balances three bronze; and one gold, one silver and one bronze together weigh $\frac{5}{2}$ kg. Find the mass of each coin type, and state what fraction of the gold coin's mass a bronze coin is.
questions.solution: With bronze = B: silver = 3B, gold = 2×3B = 6B. Sum = 6B + 3B + B = 10B = $\frac{5}{2}$ ⇒ **B = $\frac{1}{4}$, S = $\frac{3}{4}$, G = $\frac{3}{2}$ kg**. Bronze ÷ gold = $\frac{1}{4}$ ÷ $\frac{3}{2}$ = **$\frac{1}{6}$**.

questions.stem: A recipe for 6 servings requires $\frac{3}{4}$ cup sugar, $\frac{2}{3}$ cup flour and $\frac{1}{2}$ cup butter. A baker wants 15 servings but has only $\frac{5}{3}$ cups of sugar. (a) By what factor must the recipe be scaled for 15 servings? (b) How much sugar do 15 servings need, and is there enough? (c) With only the sugar available, what is the largest whole number of servings the baker can make?
questions.solution: (a) Factor = $\frac{15}{6}$ = **$\frac{5}{2}$**. (b) Sugar for 15 = $\frac{3}{4}$ × $\frac{5}{2}$ = $\frac{15}{8}$ cups; available $\frac{5}{3}$ = $\frac{40}{24}$ \< $\frac{45}{24}$ = $\frac{15}{8}$, so **not enough**. (c) Sugar per serving = $\frac{3}{4}$ ÷ 6 = $\frac{1}{8}$ cup; servings = $\frac{5}{3}$ ÷ $\frac{1}{8}$ = $\frac{40}{3}$ = 13$\frac{1}{3}$ ⇒ **13 whole servings**.

questions.stem: Find every pair of *different* unit fractions that add to $\frac{1}{2}$ with both denominators at most 6.
questions.solution: Try each smaller denominator: $\frac{1}{3}$ + $\frac{1}{6}$ = $\frac{1}{2}$ works; $\frac{1}{4}$ + $\frac{1}{4}$ is not *different*; no other choice with both denominators ≤ 6 gives a unit fraction. So the only pair is **$\frac{1}{3}$ + $\frac{1}{6}$**.

questions.stem: A fraction equal to $\frac{3}{8}$ has numerator and denominator adding to 33. Find the fraction.
questions.solution: Scale $\frac{3}{8}$ by k: $\frac{3k}{8k}$ with 11k = 33 ⇒ k = 3, giving **$\frac{9}{24}$** (which equals $\frac{3}{8}$).

questions.stem: Find all pairs of whole numbers a ≤ b with $\frac{1}{a}$ + $\frac{1}{b}$ = $\frac{1}{2}$. Show your reasoning.
questions.solution: From $\frac{1}{a}$ + $\frac{1}{b}$ = $\frac{1}{2}$ we get ab = 2a + 2b, i.e. (a − 2)(b − 2) = 4. The factor pairs of 4 give (a,b) = **(3, 6)** and **(4, 4)**.

questions.stem: Express $\frac{5}{8}$ as a sum of distinct unit fractions using the greedy method: at each step subtract the largest unit fraction that does not exceed what remains. Show the steps.
questions.solution: The largest unit fraction ≤ $\frac{5}{8}$ is $\frac{1}{2}$ (= $\frac{4}{8}$). Remainder $\frac{5}{8}$ − $\frac{1}{2}$ = $\frac{1}{8}$, already a unit fraction. So $\frac{5}{8}$ = **$\frac{1}{2}$ + $\frac{1}{8}$**.

questions.stem: A fraction has this property: adding 1 to *both* its numerator and denominator gives $\frac{3}{4}$; subtracting 1 from both gives $\frac{2}{3}$. Find the original fraction.
questions.solution: Let the fraction be $\frac{a}{b}$. Then $\frac{(a+1)}{(b+1)}$ = $\frac{3}{4}$ gives 4a − 3b = −1, and $\frac{(a−1)}{(b−1)}$ = $\frac{2}{3}$ gives 3a − 2b = 1. Solving: a = 5, b = 7, so the fraction is **$\frac{5}{7}$**. (Check: $\frac{6}{8}$ = $\frac{3}{4}$ and $\frac{4}{6}$ = $\frac{2}{3}$.)
